utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, or good afternoon already. Colonel, if I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Momcilo Bulatovic. I am one of the defence counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin. I will be asking you questions on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Sljivancanin. Could you please make a pause after each of my questions for the benefit of the record. I will try not to ask you any questions already asked by my learned friends. If there is any repetition, please don't hold it against me. Mr. Trifunovic, you are a well-respected military expert covering a number of different military areas. Do you know that -- or rather, do you know how relationships were organised in terms of issuing orders within the former JNA? Specifically are you familiar with Rule 33? Was it a matter of subordinate superior or rather younger, older or senior/junior?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it worked roughly at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber and to us what this means, subordinate/superior, what sort of relationship is that? Or junior/senior, what does that mean in terms of rank?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subordinate/superior duality is about the chain of command. It means that those subordinate unconditionally carry out any orders or assignments given by their superior. That is in terms of subordination. As for the junior/senior dichotomy, a junior officer is duty-bound to carry out any order given by a senior commander. He must also inform his own superior of this. On the condition that is, that by doing this, he would not be committing a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Rule 33 talks about these relationships within the armed forces. The superior officer is the officer who, under the law and other regulations, has the authority to command a military unit, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the law says, and that is what the rules of service stipulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A while ago we talked about these relationships based on rank. The junior/senior principle. A senior officer would be an officer holding a higher rank in relation to a junior officer, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If there are two officers holding the same rank on a given assignment, who is the senior officer?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who has a higher-level position in terms of the establishment, and who has a higher command position in terms of subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So the officer occupying a higher position, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of the establishment, a higher position, a higher-level position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, so we have this sort of situation, the one you have just described, would you then agree that a subordinate receives orders only from his own superior officer, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the only way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can a superior officer pass these orders on orally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is perfectly entitled to do both.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, can we agree on this: If an officer receives an order from someone who is his senior in terms of rank but not necessarily his superior, in this situation, in order to carry out this order, he must request authorisation from his superior and he must inform his superior about this?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he informs his superior and asks for authorisation to carry out this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, one thing I have to ask you again, is please make a pause after my question.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is duty-bound to inform his superior and to seek authorisation to carry out this specific order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What we have discussed so far, wouldn't that imply something else also, the principle of singleness of command, this is something you have explained already. Does this not imply that higher-ranking officers, officers of superior rank, must not interfere with the exercise of command by asking that officers who are not their direct subordinates carry out their orders?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But rather, these orders must be issued through the directly superior officer?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they must be issued through the directly superior officer in the chain of subordination or the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, can a junior officer, in terms of position and rank, issue an order to a senior officer in terms of position and rank?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In your capacity as military expert, do you remember any situations where this could, in fact, be the case? Perhaps I can jog your memory. Hold on a minute, please. If a superior officer was appointed the commander of a barracks or a garrison by a written order.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a more precise question. This is a whole new situation then, and a different one. If you have a junior officer who is at the aim time a superior officer, higher up in the chain of command, then he can, of course. Although he is a junior officer and if there is a written order, of course he could do that. Now that you have specified what exactly you mean, I finally understand, and the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So we have this situation: A junior officer in terms of rank is appointed commander, for example, commander of the barracks or the garrison, and then there are certain duties that are envisaged and he would in terms these duties be the superior also of those who may be his seniors in terms of rank?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now that we've raised this sort of situation; namely, a junior officer being the superior of his seniors in terms of rank, we have this situation, we have a number of similar situations. We've mentioned the situation involving a garrison commander. The position of garrison commander, could that be compared to the position of town commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is most usually the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, Mr. Trifunovic, based on the rules of service in the armed forces, can you please try to enumerate the most important duties of a garrison commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The garrison commander is normally the most senior officer or commander of the largest unit in a given town. This position entails a wide range of duties and jobs related to organising the life of the military in a given town. This has to do with order and discipline. It also has to do with general security. It also entails logistics and a number of other minor areas. Work, order and discipline, however, are the three major issues involved. Logistics is important too. And these are the responsibilities of a garrison commander. Powers are bestowed upon him to command over all barracks commanders in the area of his garrison in terms of these issues. There can be several different barracks within the area of a single garrison. But the garrison commander is the person in charge of all these various activities. There are other things, but these are the ones that I remember right now, and these strike me as the two essential issues. This is a matter of territorial competence or jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would one of the duties of a garrison commander not be to familiarise the commanders of institutions and units staying temporarily within the garrison with the rules governing order, discipline and work within the garrison?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. These are precisely the issues which all incoming commanders must be familiarised. A document is written up and it is normally passed out to even the lowest level commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is not one of the duties of a garrison commander to provide rules for work, order and discipline in the garrison's detention unit or prison?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, his duties would definitely entail that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there can be several different barracks within a garrison, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Each barracks has its own commander, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What are the duties of a barracks commander then? In relation to whoever happens to be in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duties as related to the garrison are those prescribed by the garrison commander in terms of work, order and discipline. As for duties at the barracks level, there are a number of internal duties, so to speak, in a given barracks. Work, discipline, order, barracks security and logistics for the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is not one of the duties of a barracks commander to secure order and discipline, self-protection, all sorts of internal activity, checking people who come to the barracks and those who leave, receiving visitors, and outside parties as well as arranging for places where these outside parties will meet, whoever it is that they are meeting inside the barracks?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree, Mr. Trifunovic, that these duties, which you have explained to us as being the duties of a garrison commander and barracks commander respectively, can be compared to the duties incumbent upon a town commander or local commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the issues are the same, but here we're talking about a combat operations zone. Whereas what we've been talking about so far applies to peacetime conditions. However, the duties themselves are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the beginning of these questions that I've been asking you about the superior/subordinate relationship. You explained that for us. My next question: If we have the guards brigade and the 80th Kragujevac Motorised Brigade, and these are entirely separate, can a commander from the guards brigade issue an order to someone from the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they're separate, the answer is no. They can only coordinate certain types of activity. This is usually enshrined in combat orders or any of the commander's written orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If, for example, the 80th Motorised Brigade from Kragujevac was attached to the guards brigade for coordination --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. If it is attached, then it is commanded by the commander of the guards brigade. That's it. If there is a matter of coordination, which means that there is no attachment, formally speaking, well, that's a different thing altogether. Coordination is then defined by the superior commander only in terms of whatever the relevant issues may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So that's the only situation where this applies?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I may have misunderstood one of the things you said earlier on. Mr. Trifunovic, could you please explain this, both to us and to the Chamber: Is it true that if a superior officer issues an order to a subordinate officer to do something which falls outside his remit and duties in terms of the establishment, such an order falling outside the normal remit of that soldier's duty must be given in writing specifying precisely what the duties and powers in question are?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How about this: Do you know about the brigade command and higher-level units? There are branch commanders, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who are these branch commanders, or rather let me give you a hand. Are we talking about infantry, artillery, anti-aircraft defence and the engineers, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As we have already concluded, a brigade is a joint higher level tactical unit, which has within its composition the most varied range of weapons and equipment. Branch commanders are in charge of a specific type of weapons that a brigade has at its disposal. So you are not likely to find an artillery commander unless the brigade actually has an artillery unit and the same applies to an anti-aircraft defence commander. The same applies to the engineers commander and so on and so forth. These are all technical bodies within the command. They plan operations and make proposals to the commander, the commander then tries to make a decision based on these recommendations and proposals. Most of the branches were represented in the brigades of the JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me if you know who they were subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were subordinated directly to the Chief of Staff. In the then establishment and as well as in later establishments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So in that situation when they were directly subordinated to the Chief of Staff, can the chief of the infantry branch, for example, in the brigade command the infantry battalion, or does the infantry battalion have its own commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No chief can command a unit. Only the commander can do that. We're speaking about the expert proposals to the commander in order for him to make a good decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me the status of the security organ senior officer?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of security is directly subordinate to the commander. And the security organ is within the organisation of the brigade command, so that organ is subordinated directly to the commander and not to the Chief of Staff, and the chief of security reports to the commander on all matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The work of the security organs in the then armed forces of the SFRY, was that regulated by the regulations for the work of security organs?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By the regulations for the work of security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, do you know what the powers of the security organs officers are, or if I may remind you of the rules of that service, maybe you can confirm whether that is so, and that is as follows: Senior officers of the security organs, the command units, institutions or the armed forces staff controls, in the expert sense, units of the military police. He suggests to the command senior officers units, institutions or the staff the use of units of the military police and responsible for the state and the activities of that unit. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that the security organs senior officer has no command function over the military police units?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is provided for by the rules, so I assume -- well, I don't assume, I assert that that was how it was in the field, in practice?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to now look at Exhibit 431, so could that please be placed on the screen. That's a decision of OG South commander dated of the 16th of November. In the context of this question, I would just like to clarify something. Can we look at this part that says "left boundary." This is item 3; maybe we can zoom in on that part. Just the last section of that, please. Item 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Or if you see well, Mr. Trifunovic, and see what this is about. This is an order by the OG South command of the 16th of November, 1991, where the first and second battalion of the military police are mentioned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I see 2A on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's all right then. The 1st and the 2nd Battalion of the military police. Who does a battalion of the military police receive its orders from?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the brigade commander. Here specifically it's a decision of the commander and that's how it was given its tasks in the tasks of other units as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who does the commander of the battalion issue orders to?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To commanders of companies of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And the commanders of the companies?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To commanders of the platoons and the detachments or squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree, Mr. Trifunovic, that it is -- this is precisely a confirmation of what we were talking about earlier, that command organs or senior officers of the security organs have no command functions over the units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We mentioned here the 2nd Battalion of the military police, and what I would like to ask you is if this means, or whether that refers also to any other military police unit that specifically happened to be part of OG South at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is something that pertains to any military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Trifunovic, you were at the post that you were at, and you explained what your duties and assignments were there. You saw many orders that arrived from the command of the 1st Military District, they passed through your hands, and you registered them. So what I would like to know is the following: Did you ever see an order of the superior command on the formation of OG South and an order in which the superior command appoints the command of OG South?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't it seem to you that such an order had to have been made in writing for a matter of this kind? Just answer briefly, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As a military expert, Mr. Trifunovic, and you have been in the army for a long time now, I would like to ask you to clarify some things for me now, which perhaps for us, who hail from that region, are already quite familiar. Is it correct that the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was divided into strategic operational and tactical sectors or axes?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain on what this division depended on, and perhaps tell us whether the concept of the defence and the formation of the armed forces and the concept of the country's defence boiled down to foreseeing danger of an attack by the Warsaw Pact forces and the NATO pact forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the answer. These were strategic directions based on which operational and tactical directions were then derived. So it was a question of an assessment of the threat on the territory of the SFRY as a unified area, which was covered by the JNA and the TO as its armed forces. The entire territory was divided into strategic axes or directions depending on the location and the possible operations by the enemy primarily of the Warsaw or the NATO pact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you now is if we can agree that it was precisely based on this that the armed forces were conceived, units of the JNA and that's how the strategic units were formed, so that each one could cover each particular direction?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how the strategic units were formed in order to cover the strategic axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA and the TNO. You only mentioned the JNA, but it's actually the armed forces as a whole. When I'm talking about the armed forces I do mean the entire composition of the armed forces. Based on this, can we agree, or can we conclude that there was a tactical axes, the Sid-Vukovar axes, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really be specific on that, because the strategic axes were in the depth of the territory, and they were not only changing, but after so much time has passed since I went to school, I really forgot what all of them were, so if we're talking about the Sid-Vukovar axes, well, it depends on who the aggressor was, and there of course -- it's possible that it exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And the capacities of the armed forces that were supposed to be deployed in that axis, were they determined on the basis of the significance of a particular axis?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the variety and the quality of the units and taking into account the nature of the terrain, you would use armoured or mechanised units, perhaps the air force and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, you spoke about tactical groups, operations tactical groups and so on, and here you see that it said operations group. Can we agree that an operations group is a temporary force that would cover an operations axis?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do operations groups form commands at the strategic level, and is that done by the military district or by the General Staff of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations groups are formed by commands at the operations level. So the command of the 1st Military District specifically would be the one that is involved here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But that's the strategic level.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Military District, yes, that is the strategic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the rules of the armed forces, can operations groups be made up of operations composition forces up to the strength of one or two corps, and with the rest of the attached units from the tactical composition at the rank of a brigade would be completed, would that be the composition of an operations group?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we now look at Exhibit 370? Mr. Trifunovic talked about that, but I would just like him to clarify some things in his capacity as a military expert.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not turn my microphone on. So we're talking about ERN number 0345-0009, and that is page 2 of Exhibit 370. This is not the same page. This is page 010. We need one page before that. Let me repeat. Ah, okay. Here we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, you see this list that you already had the opportunity to see. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You already answered a question by my learned friend. Which units were part of OG South, according to this chart? So we have two motorised battalions there, two battalions of the military police, of the guards brigade. Then there is a light artillery platoon, then three light artillery batteries that were added, and then another brigade, which according to the war diary entry on the 18th of November, left OG South and was replaced by the 80th Kragujevac Brigade. A battalion of the 544th Brigade, with tanks, then we have the sabotage detachment of the 93rd Protection Regiment, and there are other units there. Could you please tell me now, earlier you talked about how an operations group must be comprised of operations composition groups up to the strength of one or two corps, with attached units at the rank of brigades. According to that composition, is that what the OG South was, or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't have that strength. We were talking about a lower level. It could have been called an operations tactical group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A while ago I asked whether you had seen the decision on the establishment of OG South and its command. You said you hadn't. Have you ever seen the decision for OG South to join the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Had such a decision existed, would it have been recorded in the war diary or in the register?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have. This is the most important document in this entire situation. It should have been there, because this is the document that applies to everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a decision or an order, because that's what I think we should call it, saying that the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade had become the command of Operations Group South, a written order? Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, have you ever seen any order or report by Mr. Veselin Sljivancanin signed by Mr. Veselin Sljivancanin as the Chief of Security of Operations Group South?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any decision, report, letter, telex or anything at all in writing sent to Veselin Sljivancanin as Chief of Security of Operations Group South?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that this name, Operations Group South, is maybe not appropriate if we bear in mind the composition of that particular group. Is it perhaps possible that for security-related or other reasons maybe this name, operations group, was actually used to conceal something in terms of the forces active in the area? Would you allow for such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. To emphasise a strength that is maybe not realistic or does not tally with the reality on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could this be done in order to conceal a unit which is actually active in the area which may be some other people are not supposed to know about in a given situation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that might have been a reason too. These are assumptions. You do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Having heard all of this, Mr. Trifunovic, and once you have analysed all the documents shown by the OTP and by my learned friends from the other Defence teams, having heard everything that you have told us about the so-called Operations Group South, could we then conclude, regardless of the rules and regulations, that these forces were unified at an operative level merely to carry out a combat assignment, nothing more?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And yet, because of all the discrepancies that you have yourself observed in the various orders, in terms of how it worked, in terms of how it was organised and functioned, this was not under a single command, was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Having gone through these technical matters, I will now go back to some questions regarding Mr. Sljivancanin. Mr. Trifunovic, do you know where the security organ was physically located in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say specifically. It was in the broader Negoslavci area. The distance from the command post itself wasn't that great.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But they were not in the same place as the command post, the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the chief of security was normally there, depending on how combat activities were evolving. Usually he would have a position inside a house, but on account of the difficult conditions the command post more often than not could not be established according to the rules. One of the security organs should be at the command post and one at the rear command post. That's what the rules say. But they were in a house which was some distance from the house where the command was; operations and staff. We had to adapt to the circumstances in this settled area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We talked about the duties and the role of the chief of the security organ. What about the activities of the security body when relating to a military unit? Is there such a thing as a duty of the security organ to want to know about the security situation in a given unit, about security-related assessments? Would they not have to go directly to unit commanders for their information, would they not have to tour the units, the entire area all along the front line and the confrontation line, would they not have to go there to get their information in order to be able to do their work properly?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in purely operative terms that was normally how they went about their duties, in all sorts of situations, both peacetime and wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that this may have been one of the reasons why you, as you said, often saw Mr. Sljivancanin along the front line?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Organising the operative presence in the units is the responsibility of the chief of the security organ. This could have been often, not so often, or more often, especially if you had previously covered the ground, as it were, alongside with other operatives. This is the principle of his exercising his control of the situation. As far as I know, he did go and tour the units. He decided to do so. In terms of the unit's most motivation, I considered this to be a very good, very positive move. And this was the case also with the other units that were covered, as it were, by his fellow commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, something about the transcript, page 18, line 25. Without repeating the whole question, he said that this kind of work by the security organ applied to both peacetime and wartime, which is not reflected in the transcript. But that's what the witness said. If there is any need to go any further into that, we can ask the witness to clarify. But I think it's sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, in Vukovar you witnessed on those days several visits by both domestic and international delegations. You spoke about the visit of Mr. Cyrus Vance; you remember that, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you have such an important person visiting the area, touring the area of combat operations, what about his personal security? Would that not, in some way, be the responsibility, I mean in terms of securing the necessary conditions, security-wise, of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Regardless of the importance of that person, this applies to everybody entering the area of responsibility of that particular unit. The security organ, or, rather, the chief of the security organ is responsible for that person's security. End of story.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't answer my second question. Does this apply to everybody entering a given area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You testified about Mr. Vance's visit, and you mentioned some people who were there. Do you remember that meeting at the headquarters attended by Mr. Vance, was Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic present at that meeting too? Is this something you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my previous answer to the OTP, or to the Defence, I can't quite remember. I had the opportunity to go back to my notebook and to check who was there. And that's why I could be specific when I mentioned the people who were there. Pavkovic is not one of the names that appear. This may be an omission on my part, it's possible. But I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Dragoljub --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the last name.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about Mr. Blagoje Adzic's visit to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. The commander of the 1st Military District, Zivota Panic, yes. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again about the transcript, page 20, line 20, Dragoljub Dzukic, the last name is Dzukic. From the cabinet of the federal secretary for national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been two meetings. I only mentioned one, the one which I attended with Cyrus Vance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the arrival of the guards brigade. The assignment was to lift the blockade of the barracks. You mentioned that the start of the brigade's activity in the area was, to a certain extent, infamous because you suffered a great deal of casualties, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that during that first operation 10 soldiers of the JNA went missing who were members of the guards brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure if the figure of 10 you have mentioned is precise, but I would say roughly speaking a dozen soldiers went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was one of the duties of the security organ to gather intelligence in the field from the locals and other sources in order to try and find these JNA soldiers who had gone missing?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, do you know that on the 19th of October, 1991, a convoy carrying wounded persons left for Croatia from the Vukovar Hospital? Do you know anything about that convoy?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 19th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this convoy was organised by Medecins sans Frontieres?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do remember is the convoy organised by the humanitarian organisation known as Medecins sans Frontieres carrying food and medications, and this was supposed to be taken to the Croatian population of Vukovar, but it got stuck at the barracks. This was an incoming convoy. But I can't remember this other one; therefore, I can't answer your question. You asked me whether I remembered a convoy leaving the Vukovar Hospital on the 19th of October. The answer is I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will tell you something about this convoy, which may jog your memory, hopefully. Mr. Sljivancanin, a security officer, found a JNA soldier on this convoy who, against his own will, was about to be sent to Croatia. The soldier's name is Zivkovic. Does that jog your memory, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it does. But I can't know for certain. It's been a very long time. I remember this being mentioned, because I was privy to most of the information then, but I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would it jog your memory, in relation to these missing soldiers, those who went missing in the course of that first operation, information was obtained from the local population, and Mr. Sljivancanin, a security officer, on the 16th of November, found the remains of six burned bodies belonging to soldiers in the fighter's street in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question of -- the answer of the witness was not recorded correctly. I was talking about the remains of six soldiers who were burned, six soldiers of the JNA, and their remains were found in the street of Sremskih Boraca on the 16th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And the witness responded that he knew about this.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We heard from you, and this is also not in dispute, that on the 19th of November Sasa Jovic was taken from the Vukovar Hospital, together with another two soldiers. They were also in the group of these 10 soldiers. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, you talked about the arrival of a group of senior officers from the Security Service, three colonels, and I think you noted that down in your war diary. And you said that they stayed at the command post very briefly, and then they proceeded to their assignments. I understood that they reported to the OG commander about their assignments, they received escorts, and then they proceeded to carry out the assignments?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This was on the 19th of November in the evening?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We heard one of those people. It's -- we're talking about three colonels of the JNA. So can we conclude that this was an important, a serious group that was sent out?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my answer I emphasised that they were either from the 1st Military District or from the General Staff, which speaks for itself about their importance. And I don't know whether they were colonels. They were senior officers, but I really cannot recall their rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is clear that they were colonels, three colonels. Would the security administration send such a serious group out on some administrative tasks in Vukovar, or would they send them out to carry out a serious assignment relating to the events in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course they would be doing something from the domain of the security organs. It would be some serious assignment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Since we have an organ that sent this group out, and I'm telling you that that was the security administration, you said it was the 1st Military District or the General Staff, which is also a fairly high level, sending them out?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I said the General Staff, I would imply the administration, security administration, which is within the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, can we agree, then, that the leader of that group of security officers from the security administration was duty-bound, as part of the tasks that he was sent to execute, was duty-bound to coordinate the work of the security organs during combat operations, because of his highest rank and position there at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I concluded too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then further agree on that basis that the leader of the group of security officers from the security administration had to, once he left the combat operations zone, submit a report, a written report, about the situation he found in the combat operations zone to his superior or to the organ that had sent him to this assignment in the first place?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If anyone from that group of high-ranking officers of the security administration, in the course of executing the assignments given to them, had any kind of incident happen, had their lives happened to be in danger, if they were attacked or anything like that, or if they had issued an order to someone to do something in terms of security, their own personal security and the security of other persons or property, would that be an additional reason to be obliged to submit such a report?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something that I actually skipped in my order of questions. Before you said that at the command post there was a signals or communications centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did any orders, decisions or information arrive perhaps there in the form of telegrams?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the form of telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was anything sent in the form of coded telegrams?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, can you explain to all of us, please, what the procedure was in handling the telegrams, if you know. Was this registered in some special book or log, was there a special log-book for these telegrams precisely because of the specific way in which they were received and sent?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the communications section had its own log-book, their own separate one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On Friday during your testimony here, I heard that you had the opportunity to see in the war room the documents from Vukovar. So I would like to know if perhaps you had the opportunity to see that log-book for telegrams. Does that still exist as part of the documentation in the -- in the war room?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The period from late 1991, and the documentation in the war room, the room where the war plan is being kept, was something that was not accessible to me for a long time. Only recently was I able to gain access to the documents as part of the archives of the Vukovar operations. That should have been handed over to the military archives, but because of some objective difficulties that the minister talked about, this was not done. It is still being kept at the guards brigade premises, even though I'm retired now. Most recently, at the request of the OTP and also the Defence counsel, there were requests to review the documentation and to send some documents, and we complied with that. I stated that I was the president of the commission during the past two or three months, and that's when I went to the archives and looked at what was there. Any requests for documents were complied with. As far as this particular log-book, I really don't remember seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember Colonel Marko Maric?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain who Mr. Maric is, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Maric was deputy commander for morale and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And where was his base of operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He should have been at the rear command post, but I don't think that he was there. He was somewhere between the rear command post and the command post. But he was closer to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him at the command post?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I used to see him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about the 20th? Did you see him there or was it possible that he wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't remember seeing him on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You also said -- well, can we agree that you saw Mr. Sljivancanin very rarely at the command post?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now what I would like to ask you is the following: In response to a question by the Prosecutor, you answered that you had an entry in your war diary relating to firing corrections on the instruction of Mr. Sljivancanin. Later you said that you could not remember why you made that entry. And you talked about correcting the firing positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try to ask you some questions, and then I'm going to tell you what the position of my client is in regard to that information and that entry in the war diary. Is one of the tasks of the security organs, when touring units, and in view of the security assignments that we mentioned before, to check the security or the safety of the units at any point, and to react in case they have information from the field that, for example, the unit is in danger from artillery fire that perhaps can be a result of imprecise firing from one's own forces. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is also one of the tasks, but their assignment is to appear in units in order to monitor and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If the commander finds out about such information or receives such information, is it part of the security assignment to inform his superior that there is such-and-such a problem, and that the unit is exposed to such-and-such a danger?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If they inform the commander, would the commander then in turn inform his superior that there was a security problem for a particular unit of a particular nature?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So is the immediately superior officer, and specifically perhaps we're talking about the commander of OG South, and would he inform the commander of the 1st Military District in turn about this possibility? Would the commander of the 1st Military District then be able to ask his subordinate from whom he received that information, is it possible perhaps to have a case where there was misinformation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In order to check this information, would the commander, in this example of the 1st Military District, would send the chief of artillery to make sure at the scene whether this was actually so or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, now I would like to state the position of my client in relation to this war diary entry. The situation was that information was received during the touring of units that the artillery at positions of the 1st Military District was firing imprecisely, and that it was firing at its own unit positions, and that Mr. Sljivancanin informed the commander of OG South, and that the commander of OG South informed the commander of the 1st Military District, Mr. Zivota Panic about this. Mr. Panic received information that this information came from Mr. Sljivancanin, that he sent the chief of artillery, Colonel Grce?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Grce.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of artillery of the 1st Military District, and that at the scene they established that the artillery of the 1st Military District was firing inaccurately, that it was underfiring, short -- the fire was reaching -- not reaching the target, and that Colonel Milorad Grce then established with Mr. Sljivancanin that the problem was in damp ammunition, and this was established as the reason and that this was then used in order to make adjustments. Would you allow for the possibility that this was so?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there are different reasons to make adjustments. One of the reasons would be also ammunition, damp ammunition in this case. In order to fire accurately, it was necessary to make adjustments and the -- it was not the duty of the chief of security to order such adjustments, but it is his duty to inform about these circumstances, and if this was done along the line that you just explained, then this is correct procedure. So the chief of artillery, Milorad Grce, established the problem at the scene, and the entry in the war diary that Major Veselin Sljivancanin informed the Chief of Staff that an adjustment of artillery fire was made could have referred to the situation that you described just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have some seven minutes to go before the break. I probably won't have any further questions, but because of some technical issues that may still be open, can we please have a break now so that I may consult my client, confer with my client on a number of issues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We will adjourn now and have a half-hour break and we will resume at five minutes to 1.00. Or even five minutes to 2.00 if you like, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, I will now need to go back to one particular issue, just in order to have everything clarified. We spoke about the branch commanders, infantry, artillery, that sort of thing, and about their authority. I will now read to you from the rules of service for the security organ, Article 23, in relation to the chief of the security organ. I have read previously from the rules, but now I want to read to you two paragraphs of that article, and there is a single question that I want to ask you now. Rule 23 reads that the chief of the security organ of the unit command, the institution or the headquarters of the armed forces, exercises control in terms of technical aspects over the military police. He makes proposals to the commander of the unit, institution or headquarters on how to use units of the military police and is responsible for the condition of that unit. Article 2, or paragraph 2 of Article 23 of the rule governing the work of the security organ of the armed forces of the SFRY reads: "When exercising control over a unit of the military police, the chief of the security organ, from paragraph 1 of this Article, has the duties and responsibilities that branch commanders in the commands units and headquarters of the armed forces have in terms of exercising control over the branches, units, as well as the service and commands of units, institutions or headquarters." Mr. Trifunovic, you said you were not an expert on security-related issues. However, in your answer you explained the duties of the branch commanders, services commanders, for the brigade command and higher-level units in terms of guiding the units, from a purely technical aspect. My question is: In relation to all the other chiefs that we have mentioned, the powers of the chief of security, are they wider in scope or not? Are they bigger or smaller?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on these two articles, in terms of the comparison between the duties of the security organ in terms of control, its technical aspect and their responsibility for the situation prevailing in their units and in the branches, the powers would seem to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I have shown you an exhibit about the use of military police units showing who issues the decision. I have shown you the decision. The decision envisages certain assignments in terms of the establishment for units of the JNA. The same decisions also determine the tasks of TO units within Operations Group South, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Based on all of this, can we conclude that the security organ, or rather the commander of the security organ had no powers whatsoever over TO units in the sense of issuing orders, command and control or anything else?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is an accurate conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned at some point in your testimony Bileca and the reserve officer's college that is based in Bileca, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber that sort of a college that is. Is that an elite school training the best officers and reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is a reserve officer's college for infantry. For other branches you had schools of the same level in other places throughout the former SFRY. Artillery in Zadar, the engineering units in Karlovac and so on and so forth. This is the elite school for reserve infantry officers, the one in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You also testified about Vesna Bosanac. Where did you see her?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw her in passing, I think, on the 19th, when she came to the command post. We didn't speak, but she came to see the operations group commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this was? In the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon, possibly in the evening. I can't be specific. Once the hospital had been taken and security established, by units of the operations group, she arrived. It was dark already. The month was November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the description you provided to my learned friend, Mr. Vasic, you drew a ground plan of the command post, the rooms and who was where and that sort of thing. Mr. Sljivancanin -- if Mr. Sljivancanin had talked to her there in that building, you certainly would have seen it, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I was in the operations room at that time. But Major Sljivancanin, the commander, could have talked on that terrace, in the corridor, maybe in the working room, maybe in the commander's room where he would normally rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see Mr. Sljivancanin talk to Vesna Bosanac right there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about the media exposure that Mr. Sljivancanin got. You explained about quite a number of journalists surrounding him all the time. Can we agree that this considerable presence of journalists around Mr. Sljivancanin was caused by the fact that he was in Mr. Vance's security detail, when Mr. Adzic came he provided security, when the EU or EC, rather, observers came he was with them. He was with the ICRC people. And it was precisely because of all of this that he was so much in the public eye, and the media wanted to speak to him, right? That's what made him interesting?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I share that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that perhaps this contributed to creating this impression under the influence of the media, the impression that Mr. Sljivancanin had more importance that in actual fact he was -- he had?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So we have defined his importance on the basis of the rules and regulations that applied. However, there was the presence of media and the media's influence, which magnified his role and made it seem far more important than it actually was, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this amplified his importance, exaggerated his importance, if you like, the presence of the media. But his role certainly wasn't as comprehensive as the media would have it. Or as perhaps was the impression shared by some.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this group of officers, I said where they'd come from. Does the name of Aleksandar Vasiljevic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I think he was the chief of security of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Tumanov?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It rings a bell. I'm not really which position he held at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 34 of the transcript, line 9. Tumanov -- or rather line 11, Tumanov is the name. And the answer. T-u-m-a-n-o-v.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note, presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Based on some accounts, Mr. Vasiljevic was in Negoslavci on the evening of the 19th. He and Mr. Tumanov. Do you remember that? Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point I arrived in the guards brigade. I wasn't really particularly familiar with the structure of command from the guards brigade up, from the guards brigade level up. So I only learned later that Mr. Vasiljevic was the administration chief. I didn't know him personally. Therefore, I didn't really focus on the fact that he was the chief at the time. For an operative in terms of the security bodies of that level, I wasn't really instructed on how to handle them, how to act. I wasn't even responsible for their security detail. So before Vukovar I had never paid attention to those, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP you were asked whether you knew about the SAO Krajina government meeting that was held on the 20th of November, 1991. You said you didn't know about that. It was later on that Mr. Panic told you about such a session. What I want to know is whether he told you anything more or anything else about this session. What happened, who attended, what was debated, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not provide any details about the session or about the presence of any JNA officers, or indeed about any decisions that were or were not taken. I later heard from some officers about the decision for civilian prisoners from the Vukovar area to be handed over to TO units. I can't remember how much later or who exactly told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said you talked to Mr. Pavkovic as well, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Pavkovic perhaps tell you about what had happened at the hospital on the 20th, the 19th and the 20th?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A couple of questions to wrap things up, Mr. Trifunovic. You explained about the system of command, control, you explained about the relationships, about the importance of rank, about the importance of all the incoming groups, about the importance of the various assignments that were carried out, and so on and so forth. You spoke about the fact that the order to evacuate the hospital was not very specific, that it was very general, so to speak. You also said that the evacuation operation itself was a task of paramount importance. Can you please do this for me, sir: Try in the briefest possible terms to repeat and to clarify which were the units that would have been expected to be involved in an operation like that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the order itself did not say anything specific about the body which was responsible for this, or about how the task would be organised, this would imply that the responsibility rested squarely on the shoulders of those units who were in the area of the evacuation. Talking about the hospital itself, the units were Assault Detachment 1, and the elements of the military police battalion which took over hospital security after the hospital had been taken. Evacuation was to proceed by taking people to certain facilities and features, and then once there the commanders of those facilities and features were responsible. That is how it worked, since no detailed instructions were given. Had detailed instructions been provided, we would have known all of these things more specifically. Who was responsible, how the evacuation was to unfold, and when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree on this, sir: In terms of an operation like that, the responsible person should have been the Chief of Staff, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. The commander had sent him to the area to deal with that. And that's what the war diary reflects. He was in the area and he reported on all these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Just to wrap things up, let me ask you about the insignia worn by the forces involved in the fighting in Vukovar. Was there only one kind, or were there different kinds being worn by units?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different kinds of insignia in Operations Group South and the units that it comprised. As far as the guards brigade was concerned, they all had the same sort of insignia, depending on the type of unit. Military police units had their own military police insignia. The remaining units had the guards brigade insignia. All the other units had different insignia. Different ones for the operations group level, and for the brigade level, it depended on where the unit belonged, and this was very much complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Major Stupar from the 93rd Sabotage Detachment, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where he came from?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came from Pancevo. As to who that sabotage detachment was subordinated to, this is not something that I can say. I don't know who he was subordinated to at the time in this particular situation. In Vukovar, Operations Group South. Before being resubordinated, I think sabotage detachments would have been subordinated directly to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The General Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So the sabotage detachment was not within the guards brigade, within its composition?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question. Do you know what Mr. Sljivancanin's position is as far as the insignia worn on uniforms were concerned, the significance of the five-pointed star, which stood for Yugoslavia, the importance of Yugoslavia for him and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He cared more about this than any of us did, although we were all proud at the time, but he was prouder than any of us in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no other questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The first matter I would like to raise is in relation to Rule 90(H), and it's more specifically directed at the Defence counsel for Mr. Mrksic, and it relates to an issue that was raised in the cross-examination by Mr. Bulatovic in relation to command and control of Operations Group South. A question was put by Mr. Bulatovic stating that isn't it the case that Operational Group South was not under a single command. And if that is the case for the defence for Mr. Mrksic, I would suggest that that should be put to the witness on behalf of that accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it hasn't been put. We have rehearsed the Rule enough times for the Chamber to take the position now that if counsel are not observing the rule, they will have to suffer the consequences of it. And therefore, you've raised it now, and if it is a matter that counsel for any accused feels that they need to ask some further question about, that will certainly be allowed on this occasion. But I hope it has become entirely clear to all counsel for the Defence that their observance of the rule is a matter which is for themselves to be aware of and to suffer the consequence of if they do not observe. Therefore, I think we can dispense with what is developing into a practice of the Prosecution trying to be sure about certain things at the end of cross-examination. If the matter hasn't been clearly put, well, then, it hasn't been. And that will be on the head of the counsel who has not put it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand that that should be the practice, but because it arose out of a different cross-examination, I thought I might raise it. Your Honour, I have about 15 minutes of re-examination. I will just get the lectern.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. I can safely inform you that this process of the last week will not be repeated, it will only be for about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel, there is a few issues I would like to clarify that have arisen after the cross-examination of each of the three Defence counsel. And the first issue I would like to clarify is the issue of komandir and komandant. During the examination you discussed those principles, and I was wondering whether these principles and functions of command and control apply to both komandir and komandant. And with that I'm referring to command and control of subordinate units. Do those general principles, as you have outlined in the JNA manuals on command and control, do they apply at both levels, the battalion level and the company level?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At both levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also testified in relation to Assault Detachment 1 that you didn't know how Major Tesic commanded in his area. You presumed he formed assault groups using established companies and the detachments resubordinated to him within that area. That was a presumption on your part; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that that was how he formed the combat disposition, the assault groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But you were not aware whether, in fact, he did form those assault groups and how many; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. He could have done so in view of the force's composition. He could have formed three to five assault groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the actual formation of an assault detachment, attaching other or including other units with the battalion, would it be logical -- would it have been logical in your view for assault groups to have been formed with either -- with these other new included groups such as the TO and the Leva Supoderica group?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been logical for him to form assault groups from his subordinate establishment formations. These would be companies, so that would be those three assault groups and also to form two more from those two detachments. That would make up the three to five. Without including units belonging to the two detachments which were part of the assault groups of the establishment companies. Because it was a question of knowing the people and so on. He could have formed them from his two companies. He could have formed his two companies and those three to five assault groups. It would be logical not to include TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why would it be logical not to include TO units?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only TO units, but also not to use men from one company to another company. It's not a reliable thing to do to mix people from two companies in one assault group. He's a commander. There would be one commander, all the people in those units would know him, so it would be natural for him to assume command. Splitting up and these other subdivisions is something that would not be efficient in the execution of a combat task.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But in relation to smaller units, say smaller units than a detachment, which you referred to in your testimony as being approximately 700 under the TO structure, would it be logical to attach or include smaller units in assault groups with a company not familiar with the area?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the aspect of not being familiar with the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Does the battalion commander, and I'm referring to Major Tesic at this stage, does he have the authority to regulate the number and composition of the assault groups as an assault detachment commander, based on the regulations, to carry out any particular tasks?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the assignment from the decision of the commander, he would receive his zone axis and objective. And on the basis of the rule that you mention, everything else would be up to the commander. He would be responsible for implementing the assignment efficiently. So for the purposes of carrying out an assignment received from the commander, he would be able to form his forces in accordance with the principles, which I mentioned, and applying all the principles of command and control that we also discussed. A commander would not permit any major mistakes in this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So in relation to the forming of assault groups, are you saying that the assault detachment commander has a degree of independence in how those groups are set up?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as forming groups in his own detachment is concerned, there he has the initiative and can act independently. I think that that's clear. There are three elements that he receives from the commander; the objective, the zone, and the axis. Also the time by which the task is to be completed. So in line with all of that, he would draft the schedule or deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best deployment, as far as I'm concerned as battalion commander would be to have three assault groups from establishment companies and two assault groups comprised of the assault detachments. And in that case you could use the TO forces. I don't know what he did in this specific case, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know whether Captain Radic was the commander of an assault group? Or not.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the komandir of a company, under the assumption that this was how he formed the assault groups, which would be logical, Radic should have been the commander of an assault group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, please. There has been a mistake in the transcript. On page 42, line 19, the witness said that in any -- that any assault group can include a guide of the TO, and in the transcript it says forces of the TO. And this is a significant difference. So perhaps we could ask the witness again whether he said that besides the company members the group could include a guide from the TO, and not forces from the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Smith, you might, I think, clarify what was the view expressed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, when you answered the question about assault groups and who could -- what units could be within an assault group, are you saying that TO -- a TO unit could be placed within an assault group, or a TO guide, a Territorial Defence guide? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I said that I don't know how he set up the combat disposition. But if I were a commander it would be logical for me to make the following disposition: Three assault groups from establishment companies and with guides from the TO detachments linked to certain axes and then to form two more assault groups from the forces of the Territorial Defence.
