I would not reinforce the assault groups by using the personnel from TO forces. But I say again I don't know what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But nevertheless, there is nothing in the brigade battalion rules or regulations relating to the prohibition of using TO members in assault groups; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I was talking about the principle that units of the Territorial Defence or units of the JNA would usually remain as an establishment entity in order to carry out a combat task. So an establishment entity should be issued an assignment in order to implement a decision by the commander. It is never a good thing to transfer personnel from a different establishment formation into another establishment formation. So it's not logical to move men from company to company, or from Territorial Defence to a company, with the exception of guides, who would be from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You also testified that as Tesic, Commander Tesic, as the assault detachment commander, he had de jure and de facto control over the Territorial Defence in the assault detachment and the Leva Supoderica unit, which were subordinated to the Assault Detachment 1. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And who was in the sector of operations of Assault Detachment 1, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Does that principle of command and control, having de jure command and de facto command and control over units in the assault detachment, would that also apply to the commander of an assault group if units were placed within that assault group, that the assault group commander would also have de jure and de facto control over units?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this question is not articulated enough, because we did have the answers what it means in a specific situation to replenish companies, assault groups, with other military force members. If we ask the witness if the TO was in a company, is the commander authorised de jure and de facto, this question then is more than leading because we heard from the witness that by establishment a whole TO unit cannot be placed in a company, and then use that as an assault group. The witness said that on a number occasions. It seems to me that this was perhaps a trick question, so I would like to have a more specific question put so that the witness could provide a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. But I think the witness has demonstrated he is very well capable of not being fooled by such questions, if there was any danger of it. And I think, can be left safely to deal with the issue. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, in this case, there is evidence that Captain Radic stated that: "At one point there are about 500 people of different nationalities and with different party affiliations in the company which I commanded. They were active service men, volunteers, Chetniks and Serbian volunteers. I had to unite them under within command to ensure success. That day 44 volunteers left my unit. A unit of 300 soldiers remained, and we reorganised it. We formed an assault platoon, which was tasked with raiding houses" -- There is an objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems to me that nobody actually mentioned this so far, not in the examination-in-chief or in the cross-examination. So I think that this might be exceeding the bounds of what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My recollection is the same as yours, Mr. Borovic, that this hasn't been specifically raised. But the issue is very much raised by the general course of some cross-examination. So I would allow this passage of evidence to be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And on that point, it hasn't been provided as oral evidence, but it's an exhibit, and it's Exhibit 353, which was tendered through a witness, that particular interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, the passage that I just read out to you relates to an alleged admission by Captain Radic that he commanded 500 people at one point in time, and then later 300 people, and those people included the company, volunteers, reservists, et cetera. Assuming that these facts are correct, what would you classify this unit of 500 and then 300 people in military terms, what would you classify that unit as? What type of unit would it be?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the level, it would be from the battalion to the company level. It started out as a battalion and ended up at the level of the strength of a company. So not going into this admission that you just talked about, it should be clear that as commander of a company Radic had an active strength of peacetime army, as well as the reserves, and this was an establishment company of the 1st Battalion of the Guards Motorised Brigade. TO units, if the major part of them were not resubordinated to Captain Radic by a decision of the commander, then the numbers would not be very large. The volunteers that you mentioned could have, according to the decision of Major Tesic, commander of assault group 1, been completely attached to Captain Radic, or could have been distributed among the three assault groups that existed in the area of operations of Assault Detachment 1. So it's not clear to me, this reduction now, from a battalion going down to 300, why was this reduction in numbers happening. That's something that I don't have an answer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. But in relation to terms such as assault groups and assault detachments, this group of 500, then 300, would they be classified as assault detachments or assault groups? Or something else?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 500 strength would be classified as a -- an assault detachment. It was not classified like that probably by decision of the commander of the Assault Detachment 1. This deviates from the principles, but this is possible in conditions that prevailed in Vukovar at that time. It's possible that the strength was at the number of an assault detachment, but that it was called an assault group. There was a period when the numbers or the strength changed, but this is something that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You testified that the Territorial Defence detachments, under the normal rules, would have a manpower of about 700 people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And on that basis, I think your evidence is that an assault detachment of that size would not be included within an assault group, because of the sheer size; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also testified that the Petrova Gora TO, Territorial Defence, had about up to 150 to 200 men in it, whilst in Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. At the beginning though. But the arrival of volunteers, such as volunteers from Seselj's party who had joined, could have been regulated in the sense that some of them would be in Leva Supoderica, and others would be placed in the other assault groups. So I'm not clear about the -- the effect the volunteers had on the overall numerical strength because I don't know exactly how many volunteers joined the assault detachment. Assault Detachment 1 was the strongest one, because it also had another two TO units. The others were at the establishment level of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say what the size of the Leva Supoderica unit was in terms of men?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number because I assume that the detachment did not comply exactly with the regulations like the Petrova Gora detachment did in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the -- the admission or the alleged admission as to the size of the unit that Captain Radic commanded, and the fact that the Petrova Gora TO detachment was a lot smaller than 700, would it be fair to say that the normal principles that would apply in the manuals as to the size of assault groups and size of assault detachments didn't necessarily apply accurately to the situation in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The specific situation allowed for the possibility to accept something like that regardless of the fact that it was not something that complied with the principles or regulations. The decision of the commander of OG South was not along the lines of forming two assault detachments from that assault detachment, even though that was the numerical strength of the assault detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in response to a question by Mr. Borovic, you stated that companies don't have headquarters but they have observation posts in combat operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the situation where an assault group commander would plan activities, that particular location, what type of -- what type of place would you call that? An observation post or something other?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's always an observation post by the company commander. The planning level that he is involved at is such that he assigns tasks in the field. From one to three points.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what type of assistance a company commander has or an assault detachment -- sorry, an assault group commander has, in combat operations? You said that a headquarters, command headquarters would have staff, but an observation post won't have staff. Does a company commander have some assistance that would otherwise be classified as staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A battalion command has several officers attached to the command. The commander, his deputy, the assistant commander for morale guidance, the assistant commander for logistics. These would be the battalion-level officers. This is a sufficient number of officers for an assault detachment commander to have at his disposal, and in order to send one to each of the assault groups, while giving out assignments and carrying them out. This is from the point of view of the battalion, and this is how it's done. That's part of the principles of command. From the point of view of a brigade or an assault detachment, these teams are sent to the battalion command, their objective being to monitor the situation in the battalion and to focus on those areas where a problem is being dealt with in order to achieve a certain objective. One from the brigade, up to two in the battalion, the assistance, the assault detachment, one of these two could be in one of the assault groups, if that's where the focus lies. And from the battalion another one or two officers. So in practical terms, more officers from the brigade, the battalion, or rather the assault detachment. There shouldn't be more. Therefore, no chance of setting up a headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the assault group and assuming the assault group was the size of 500 to 300 people, what type of assistance would you expect an assault group commander of that size would be present, or would there be any to assist in the functioning of that assault group?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I might just prove right this time around. My learned friend has said a number of times we have Radic's admission that so and so. We don't have any admissions whatsoever. But the witness said that 500 men could not amount to anything else but an assault detachment. We can't just conveniently forget about that and ask what sort of support might an assault group comprising between 300 and 500 men be enjoying. My learned friend should follow closely what the witness is saying in the interests of both the OTP, I believe, and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe I have been following it quite closely. The witness stated that in Vukovar the sizes of assault detachments and assault groups were not as normally would be regulated for, and I thought it was a reasonable question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not suggesting that you should not put it. Put in that form whether or not it is of use to us depends then upon the findings we make about disputed factual matters. But that's an ordinary feature of litigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, regardless of whether a group is called an assault group or an assault detachment, if a man is placed in charge of a group of 500 to 300 people in combat operations, what type of assistance would you expect that commander to have, what type of assistance in terms of people?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of numerical strength, he should have some. But a numerical strength of that order of magnitude is probably a result of the area to be covered and the objective. If this was the same numerical strength as prevailed in all the other assault groups of this assault detachment, then the focus of any assistance should be on that particular assault group. What can be expected of this sort of assistance. Assistance can be expected from the battalion command. One or two most senior officers, perhaps even the battalion commander himself, or the assault detachment, along that axis. That much and not more. Because there are no resources at the battalion command level left to do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to turn to another topic, and it relates to the strength of the Operational Group South's units in their zone of responsibility, and earlier you were shown by my learned friend Mr. Vasic an exhibit, and the exhibit Number was 370, and it related to the composition of Operational Group South as of the 16th of November. In that quite long list, you saw a number of battalions present in the disposition of Operational Group South. Do you remember seeing that document? It had quite a number of pages. Or the English did.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In that document it didn't include the Petrova Gora Territorial Defence unit, or any Territorial Defence unit for that matter, nor did it include the Leva Supoderica unit. Can you explain why those units didn't appear in that disposition sheet and yet you stated earlier that they were in the zone of responsibility of Operational Group South?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the overview that was sent to the superior command was in relation to JNA units. The JNA units involved. I can't remember if other commanders contributed their own reports about any TO units to that overview. I should have a look perhaps, but my assumption is, if they're missing from the overview, then probably an overview was requested in relation to JNA units only. And then this is exactly what was submitted to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to talk about the Vukovar Territorial Defence. And you mentioned earlier in your testimony in cross-examination that Miroljub Vujovic was appointed the Territorial Defence commander for Vukovar on the 20th or the 21st of November, as you were asked to draft an order to that effect by Colonel Mrksic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I stated is correct. I was tasked with drafting this order. The order was signed, whether on the 20th or the 21st, I really can't remember. When did it take effect, likewise. Probably right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also stated that it was unusual that Colonel Mrksic had the ability to appoint a Territorial Defence commander as opposed to a civilian authority. Can you explain why it was unusual for --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There is an objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe my learned friend has either inaccurately remembered or misinterpreted what the witness said. He said he had no legal option open to him to appoint a Territorial Defence staff commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can't say I remember the evidence, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On that particular point, I mean, in terms of the use of the word "ability" I was using that in more of a general sense rather than necessarily a legal ability. That's what the follow-up question was about, as to why he thought Colonel Mrksic didn't have the ability or did have the ability to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're talking practical ability or legal power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Both. Initially practical ability, and then I was going to discuss the matter of legal power, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In times of combat action, all sorts of actions and steps must be taken. And often when the dust settles you then sort out the technicalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you're talking legal power, make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, at the time that Colonel Mrksic issued or asked you to draft that order appointing Miroljub Vujovic as the Territorial Defence commander, is it the case that you -- that you did not believe that he had a legal power to do so or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did not have the legal power to do so. I said when Mr. Vasic asked me that I had been greatly surprised at the time, but I had no opportunity to go any further into the essence of the relevant laws and regulations. I had no time to warn him either. That was the order that I received, and I assumed at the time that this was in keeping with the relevant laws and regulations. Although it did occur to me at the time that maybe it wasn't after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In peacetime who would be the appropriate body that would appoint a Territorial Defence commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about who was in charge of the TO. This depended on the level. The socio-political community, the socio-political organisation, the municipality, the republic, and that was the highest level of command over the TO. It was the TO HQs that normally had a commander, since, at the time for a while there was an HQ and then it was disbanded, and then the government of the SAO Krajina set up an HQ, and then the commander of that HQ would have been responsible for appointing -- or, rather, the government would have been responsible for appointing an HQ commander. In case of the TO, this was Miroljub Vujovic. However, as far as I remember, there was no agreement back then to appoint Vujovic TO headquarters commander, but rather to appoint him commander of Vukovar's TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The fact that Colonel Mrksic asked to you draft that order, would that indicate that there was no proper functioning civilian authority at that time and he did that as a result of exercising his military authority to do so?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In response to -- just moving to a different topic now, but in response to a question by my learned friend, Mr. Bulatovic, he asked you whether or not Operational Group South -- he stated that Operational Group South didn't have a single command during these combat operations, and you replied yes. In your examination-in-chief, you discussed on numerous occasions through the documents, through the orders, that Colonel Mrksic was the Operational Group South commander for that -- for that zone of responsibility, and all units, JNA units and Territorial Defence units, were included in his command. Can you explain what you meant by Operational Group South not having a single command? It's a little bit unclear.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Bulatovic was the one who asked this question. He asked was there an order appointing the command of the guards brigade as the command of Operations Group South. My answer was I didn't remember such an order. My answer was I hadn't seen any such order. Therefore, there was nothing in writing appointing Colonel Mrksic commander of OG South, or at least I didn't see anything like that. Unless he received an oral appointment by the 1st Military District who was the superior of the guards brigade and OG South, General Panic. This was not done properly, because there had to be something in writing. If the command of the guards brigade took over command of OG South, all I can say is that both in terms of manpower, in terms of everything else, it was perfectly able to command all other units within the operations area. And I think that was precisely what it did, at least in as far as unity of command was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I wonder whether your question there has confused two different ideas and two different threads of evidence. I thought the proposition you quoted from the evidence was related to the fact that there was a forward command post and another, and there wasn't a single command in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I may have -- I may have misinterpreted that -- that answer in that sense, but just on the basis that I didn't, I just wonder if I could continue with one last question on the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Certainly, Colonel, for the period of time that you were in Vukovar in the combat operations there, did you hear of anyone challenging Colonel Mrksic's command as Operational Group South commander or challenge its authenticity or legitimacy?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear anything like that, nor did I myself wonder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one last topic; it's in relation to Major Sljivancanin. In relation to the evacuation of people from the Vukovar Hospital on the 20th of November, 1991, were you aware what Major Sljivancanin's role was?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly. I did not know anything about the communication between him and the commander. I was never present. In that one answer I said it would have been logical for the Chief of Staff to be the person responsible for that evacuation. It would have been logical. However, there was no order to that effect. I said my assumption was that Colonel Mrksic may have ordered this to the Chief of Staff orally. There was an on-site report saying that the Chief of Staff was there, and that there was a certain amount of difficulty that they encountered. I had no clear idea of Mr. Sljivancanin's place in this whole thing, but there was that visit by the three security officers and I sort of thought that this had to do with the mission that they had. They were there to check how the evacuation was going, whether it was all right, whether it was proceeding in an organised manner, and that their remit was to inform their superiors about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. And it is important that we are clear that we're separating what you factually knew to some logical speculation that you might have. In relation to Major Sljivancanin's tasks throughout the Vukovar operation, were you aware of what his particular tasks were?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the security organs tasks in very general terms. Operative and security activities covering the unit in terms of security, in terms of inspections, in a very general sense. But I didn't know at the time what its specific tasks were, nor was it really part of my training.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Colonel, the last question, the chain of the -- the reporting chain of command between Major Sljivancanin and Colonel Mrksic, did that include anyone else, apart from those two people?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was direct contact between the two. There was no one in between, in terms of the chain of command. When I said that the chief of security was directly subordinate to the commander, this means there are no go-betweens, no middlemen in that chain of command. How the two of them established communication, how they communicated, is not something that I can talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I have finished the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Colonel, there is just one little thing which has come to the eye of the Chamber. Do you have the folder with you still? Tab 10, Exhibit 401. I can only refer to the English version of it, but there are two entries appearing on page 39 of the English translation of the war journal. One for 2355 hours on the 17th of November, and the other just a couple of hours later, 0140 hours on the 18th of November. They're successive entries, so one is the last entry for the 17th of November, and the other is the first entry for the 18th of November, if that helps you find it in B/C/S. But I must say, I couldn't find it as I looked through the B/C/S. One refers to: "The duty team (Lieutenant-Colonel Lesanovic)," and that's the first entry at 2355 hours. The entry at 0140 hours on the 18th refers to Lieutenant Lesanovic. And the question is whether they are the same person with somebody omitting to put in colonel or putting in a colonel too much, or were these two different people? One is described as Lieutenant-Colonel Lesanovic; and the other as Lieutenant Lesanovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have found that. I found the entry. 2355 hours, the 17th of November. We are talking about Lieutenant-Colonel Lesanovic, who was the chief of the rocket artillery units of the anti-aircraft defence. Could you please point me to the other entry that you have mentioned, since I can't remember which one it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... exactly the one following at 0140 hours on the 18th. And it starts -- it's speaking about Marin Vidic telephoning. But at the very end of it, it refers to Lieutenant Lesanovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have found it. The leader of the duty team, Lieutenant-Colonel Lesanovic, scheduled the conversation for 0800 hours on the 18th. So we are dealing with the same person in both these cases. And the rank is lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems in the English translation the word "colonel" was left out of that second entry. It's no greater mystery than that. And he was a commander of the -- you mentioned where he came from. A battery, was he? He was from artillery? Lieutenant-Colonel Lesanovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Lesanovic was attached to the staff of the guards brigade command. He was the chief of rocket artillery units of the anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, thank you for that. It seemed a mystery if they were two different people, but they are the same person, and he was then the leader of the duty team over that night. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Colonel, you will be pleased to know that's the end of your evidence. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance and thank you very much for the assistance that you have given. I know it's been a long time in the witness box, but we are grateful for the attention you paid to your evidence. You may now, of course, be free to go back to your retirement occupations, whatever they are. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Looking at the clock, Mr. Smith/Mr. Moore, I think it may be a convenient time now to have the break. And we will no doubt resume with a new witness after the break. We will resume at a quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand a matter is to be raised in the absence of the next witness. Is it Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. Good afternoon. I am representing all three Defence teams, and we asked the witness not to be here, because we would like to inform you about one thing that is of concern and interest to us. While reading the transcript from the testimony of this witness before the Belgrade court, he testified that he kept the work book which, as an officer of the JNA he had with him at the time during the combat operations in Vukovar. Previously we received parts of the notebook, of which certain lists are a part of, but when we found out from the Prosecution that he had kept the entire work book with him, in January, at a meeting with the OTP, we asked our learned friends from the Prosecution to allow us to look at the whole work book. We also informed the OTP about that about 10 days ago when we found out this witness was coming to testify, and we were informed by Mr. Moore that he had provided us with relevant parts of the work book, that he had looked at the entire work book and believes that we were given the relevant parts. We believe that as the Defence we do have the right to have the whole book for our purposes, and we believed that that was also what we had in mind when we informed the Prosecution about that in January, before we learned that the witness was coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't see any problem. We have given copies to my learned friend of all material that we believe is relevant. I think it's 17 pages from his notebook. It's 65 ter exhibit number 125. We didn't have the original itself; we had only the photocopy. I have spoken to the witness in relation to the document. It is his own private document. I asked him whether there was any other material over and above that which we have disclosed. Then I asked him whether it was relevant to the matters. And as far as I can see from the dates, there are certain entries, I think, in relation to the 21st, but not in relation to his evidence in relation to this matter. It involves other inquiries. So we have fulfilled our obligations, as we believe them to be, and it is a matter for the individual concerned, namely the witness, whether he is willing to disclose matters on other topics that are confidential and to which he is privy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the Prosecution has had the full document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, we have not had the full document, but we have had it for six days, and there is other material in it, but it does not relate to the evidence that this witness is giving. He was a military policeman, and it relates to other inquiries, as far as I am concerned. Because clearly if a document is here and it's relevant, the Defence should see it. I have no problems with that. But equally, I must balance his right to privacy for other material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think it's a matter for the Prosecution to determine that, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One standing at a time, Mr. Lukic. If would you sit, please. Yes. The issue will be for the Chamber to be satisfied whether there is material elsewhere in the notebook that is relevant to the witness and the evidence he gives in this case. That is something that it may be necessary for the Chamber to take a little time over. Because undoubtedly it will be in handwriting and undoubtedly not in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is correct. It is not a large notebook. There is not a large amount of material. It is dated, moving away from the time-span of which this witness gives evidence, and then there is other inquiries in relation it other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That may make it quite a bit easier for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Lukic, was there something more you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to note just one thing. These are not private notes, and it's not the witness's private document. This is a notebook that each JNA officer has with him, carries with him, the pages are marked, and at the end of a task or service the officer is obliged to present that document to the unit archives. He said at the Belgrade hearing that he knew that but he did not do that. So we cannot treat that as a personal document. It's an official document, and we could not have requested it in any other way other than through the Prosecution. And we did that back in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't know why my learned friend is making a great fuss about it. I have told the witness to bring it to Court, it is available for the Defence. If they asked to see the document, it is available. There is no difficulty at all. So I do not know why my learned friend is objecting in the way he is. The document is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying that the witness has no objection to Defence counsel viewing the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The witness was slightly ambivalent in relation to the document itself. I do not find him to be a difficult man in any way at all. He takes the view that it if the Defence wants to see the document and they ask questions in relation to it, I do not detect that he will try and retain the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would suggest not only was he perhaps a little ambivalent, but your submissions to the Chamber earlier were equally. Because I understood from them that the witness regarded it as something that should not be disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Only to the extent that he says it does not relate at all to the matter at Vukovar and the incident at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is for that reason that it seemed to me that what you were posing was a problem that had to be resolved by the Chamber viewing the document and deciding whether parts of it only should be disclosed, or the whole. But from what you say, that is unnecessary because the witness will allow the document to be made available overnight to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the other matter that I was going deal with, if it is of any interest to my learned friends, the pages are numbered, and there are certain numbers that I was going to deal on the ELMO with the pages, as it were, following the relevant date, and my learned friend can see it. So there is no difficulty as far as the Prosecution is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. By the sound of it, the problem may be evaporating as we talk about it, Mr. Lukic. But we will see. The witness will be called, will give his evidence in chief. If it is pertinent, the document, it seems, can be viewed by counsel overnight. But as it's dated and as it seems to relate to a variety of different inquiries, it may be that it will not take a great deal of time for counsel to examine it. We will see. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I call the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that's given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What is your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Vezmarovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: 2nd of December, 1952.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I was going to lead the witness on the first two pages and then move on to the third paragraph of the third page. I presume, as it only relates to background, there will be no objection to that course. Is it right that you were a reserve captain in the 80th Motorised Brigade of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you described the function that you had as a commander of the military police company of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, please, with the various courses that you attended to prepare you for being involved with the military police? Now, what courses did you attend, please? Just in very general terms.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: The first part of training was conducted in Bileca in 1977 and 1978, that is the school of non-commissioned officers. After that I spent one month in Pancevo, and my last period in the army was in Podgorica. After that I was trained as commander of a military police platoon. In the following period, I went to Pancevo for additional training as a commander of a military police company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what sort of work do the military police actually do within a brigade, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: The military police basically secure the commander at location and during movement, security for its own unit, and then for all other tasks and assignments received from the commander, combat or fighting terrorist groups, guarding prisoners of war, guarding problematic conscripts in local units, and all the other assignments as ordered by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we deal with 1991, I think it's right to say that you were called up on two occasions, between the 17th and 24th of September, 1991, and between the 7th and 17th of October, 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In furtherance of that, I think it's equally correct to say you were called to various locations in Serbia, where certain exercises were carried out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that period, there were mobilisations on the territory of the Republic of Serbia, and we were exercising in order to be prepared for any eventual incidents, and we were receiving a kind of refresher training covering things that we had already been trained in before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal, please, with your commander of -- your commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade at that time was Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You described it as having very little direct contact, direct contact or command link with him. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in actual fact, your direct command link was to Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Jeftic, who was the security officer at that brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Excuse me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that the witness can be led through the biographical information, but I would like the Prosecutor not to lead on questions pertaining to the direct chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you the question then, please, who were you directly -- who did you directly communicate to at brigade level?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: The security organ in Kragujevac, that was Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic, and later when we left Kragujevac, if he wasn't there, then it was Dragi Vukosavljevic, Captain First Class, in the security organ. So the security organ was the organ that I communicated with if there was no more direct communication with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why did you communicate with the security organ, can you explain to us why, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: The security organ, according to the chain of command, is responsible with work -- for work with the police company. So that lieutenant-colonel was in charge of the military police company, when we were in Kragujevac, and also for its engagement. When Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic wasn't there, then Captain First Class Dragi Vukosavljevic was in charge. Simply speaking, according to the chain of command, the security organ, was my direct or my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you, that's very clear. Can I deal, please, with the theoretical and the actual. In theory, what was the numbering of personnel within a reserve military police company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Theoretically during mobilisation we were supposed to call up between 80 and 90 conscripts according to the establishment. But in practice, depending on the time the exercises were held, we never had a fully staffed -- 100 per cent fully staffed unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If one was trying to estimate from recollection the number that you had within your military police company, how many men did you actually have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood the question properly, in 1991, when we set off for Vukovar, if that's what the question refers to, there were about 70 soldiers engaged, 70 of them responded -- had responded to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say that you described it in your statement including officers, policemen, drivers, paramedic and other support personnel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A military police company does not only include recruits trained as military police officers, it also comprises several platoons of transport personnel, that is the part that goes with the command, including drivers who are in charge of vehicles. So that was the number of people who had responded to the call-up of various profiles. They were recruits that had belonged to the atomic, chemical and biological protection, the medical services and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's also right to say that you have described in your witness statement that you had a deputy, that you had four officers, two of whom were platoon commanders, and one was a traffic police commander, and one was in charge of logistical supplies. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, in your witness statement you give a list of the sort of tasks that you performed as military police. I just want to deal with one in particular. You refer to securing military prisons. Now, can you explain what you mean by that, please, in what I will call a combat scenario?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: A military police company is obliged also to have a prison where it can put a certain number of prisoners. If we're talking about a larger group that cannot be accommodated in that facility, then it is obliged to find a space where this larger group can be secured and guarded. We had a small prison in Negoslavci, it was an improvised facility, but it did have all the required conditions to be a prison. Military police also secures and guards that kind of prison facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In your witness statement you say the following: "In combat situations the military police were also tasked to deal with prisoners of war." Now, what was the general tasking in relation to dealing with prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: One of the assignments of military police is to guard prisoners of war while they are at a location and also during movements. At a certain period of time in Vukovar, it was our task to guard the prisoners at certain locations. So my unit was in charge of guarding prisoners at a camp, if I can call it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And to what extent are the security organs involved in that particular function?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: If it is the security organs you have in mind, it works like this: If I don't have a direct order from my commander, then it's the security organ that tells me what to do or how I should act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will come back to this topic in due course. I think it's right to say on the 7th of November you were called up again. The 8th of November you left your location I think at 9.00 in the morning, and you were ordered to go to the village of Negoslavci. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say that you believe you arrived at 1400 hours, and that you reported to Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, who was already at that location. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's also right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you report to Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic was the commander of the unit. He was the person I was supposed to report to, to tell him that we had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you, in very brief order, please, tell us what happened when you arrived at Negoslavci? Can you give us a picture of what occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: The moment I reported to Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic he gave me the task of putting a unit up in an unfinished house near the command location. The next thing was to have the unit accommodated in that building to park the vehicles to set up a security regime for the unit, and other issues to do with the commander's security in that area, to replace those people who had been with them for some time with new military policemen. I'm not sure if this is relevant, but the next thing that happened was we had to secure some accommodation and some food. We needed supplies, we needed to secure everything that was necessary for the unit to go on functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say that you stayed at Negoslavci or in Negoslavci for several days and carried out what you would perhaps consider to be normal duties; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I deal, please, with what I will call areas of responsibility. The time came, I think, that you were attached to a particular group involving an area of responsibility. Can you assist us with to whom that refers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We know, for example, that there was OG South and there was OG North. To whom were you attached?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: I was attached to the 80th Motorised Brigade, and we were part of OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal then, please, with the actual command post in Negoslavci? Did you visit the command post at Negoslavci on a regular basis or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: The command post was two houses further down the street from our own location. I would go there several times a day, for a variety of reasons, normally. Sometimes they called me about something or I was just passing by. So I would just drop in on them to check if everything was okay with the soldiers securing the command post. To check if there needed to be a better rotation system in terms of who was on duty. To see if the commander was planning on leaving the command post, in which case I had to secure a sufficient number of military policemen who would escort him while he was moving around. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to assist the Court that whilst you were at the command post did you see any of these defendants there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, there were a lot of officers there for all sorts of reasons, I assume. I can't be very specific as to whom exactly I saw there, but people were saying that Captain Sljivancanin would come every now and then. People were saying that he was there, around somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with the 18th of November, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, before you move on, could we be sure of the unit of which this command post was the command post?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We referred to command post at Negoslavci. To which unit was it a command post of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: It was the command post of the 80th Motorised Brigade. My unit. That is the command post that I have been talking about. I have been talking about the 80th Motorised Brigade and our command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the command post of OG South?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: I think that I went on the 19th of November, the morning of the 19th. If that was what the command post of OG South really was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to just slow down now, if I may. And I want to deal with the 18th of November. I think it's correct to say that Colonel Vojnovic called you and informed you that you were going to have to deal with prisoners of war from Vukovar and secure them. I want to deal with that day and that particular indication from Vojnovic. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As a result of that information, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic called me and told me that it was expected that we would have to secure a large group of POWs from Mitnica, people who had surrendered. He said we should look into the possibilities of where to put them up and that we would be securing them until they were evacuated eventually. That morning the two of us, alongside with a group of other officers and soldiers, set out to inspect the area to see if we could find any appropriate buildings that we could use for this purpose, to secure those POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say "appropriate buildings," what do you mean by appropriate buildings in that context?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: In order to set up a security regime for a large group of people, we had to find an appropriate building or an appropriate facility. Given the weather conditions at the time - it was late November - there was a lot of rain and snow. The temperatures were extremely low already. Also in terms of the POWs trying to escape, and it was also about the number of men that we needed in order to carry out an assignment like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, did your travels take you to Ovcara, amongst other locations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ovcara is a facility that we passed very often. We didn't know what its condition was precisely. I'm talking about the buildings there. So we went to Ovcara to check the condition of those buildings, whether the roofs were in place, whether you could actually get into the buildings, whether the prisoners could be put up there in an appropriate manner, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you come to a conclusion about a suitable location for those prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The hangar struck us as quite solid, at least half of the building was in satisfactory condition. We decided to use that area to get the commander to give us an order to clear a portion of the hangar. There was a lot of hay all over, and we had to get the area ready for the POWs so that they could get on with their lives there. We didn't know how long they would be staying. An hour perhaps, perhaps even longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Had you any indication at that time how many prisoners of war would be coming under your control?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Not in terms of really knowing how many people we were to expect. All we knew was there would be a large group of people arriving. The hangar struck us as satisfactory, even for a group potentially larger than the one you specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How many doors or operational doors were working at Ovcara at that time; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: If it is the hangar that we selected that you have in mind, there were doors in the other section of the hangar that couldn't be used. The first door we came across we immediately tried to mend so that they could be open and should without difficulty. We needed to be able to shut the door both because of the possibility of escape and also on account of the weather conditions. It was bitterly cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, you've said that you chose this location. Did Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic agree with the choice of this location?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Completely. He ordered me to clear the room and to prepare it for holding POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: After the hangar had been chosen, did you then return to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we all returned to Negoslavci. I took along a group of soldiers and some equipment, and we were off to clear the hangar. We took all the hay from that section of the hangar across to the opposite end of the building. We found quite a considerable amount of ammunition there while clearing. We concluded that some soldiers had been sleeping there. We cleared the area as best we could, and at least half the overall area of the hangar was put into a satisfactory condition to hold POWs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you were at Negoslavci, were you informed when the group of prisoners would be coming to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: No. Once I had finished clearing the room, I went back to Negoslavci. In a way, we prepared the building for their potential arrival. We didn't really know for certain at the time whether they would be arriving or not, but everything was ready for them. The group's arrival was eventually announced at 1600 hours, or thereabouts. It was about half an hour previously that I had left Negoslavci again to go back to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can we deal now, please, with your evidence about when you returned to Ovcara and the arrival of the prisoners of war? So can we deal with that area, please? So did you see the -- the prisoners arrive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had already been at Ovcara for about 20 minutes by the time the group arrived. They arrived on buses and were escorted by military vehicles, Puch, P-u-c-h, and Pinzgauer. They stopped outside the hangar, and the military vehicles disgorged a number of military officers. I don't remember exactly who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal with the convoy itself. You've told us about Puch vehicles and Pinzgauers. How many buses arrived with prisoners of war inside? Can you remember, can you give us a clue, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: It was a drawn-out convoy of vehicles, about three or four buses possibly, the way I remember. The rest were military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us three or four buses. How many military vehicles do you think there was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: There were military vehicles escorting the buses. They didn't park on the road itself, they parked by the roadside, and the only vehicles left on the actual road were the buses. That's at least as far as I'm able to remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if you have a convoy of prisoners of war, is it normal or abnormal to have military vehicles accompanying the convoy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Military vehicles are supposed to secure that sort of convoy. Rather, the military police with their military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why is that? Can you explain to us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the task of the military police. They have to secure the person of the commander, both when mobile and when stationary, but they also have the duty to protect prisoners, and these were prisoners being moved from one location to another. And it was for that reason that they were being escorted by military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You are a military policeman. To what extent is the security situation of prisoners of war paramount when you are considering allocating military police vehicles and/or military policemen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about my own unit. We had Pinzgauers. Pinzgauers are vehicles that are relatively easy to manoeuvre. And they can normally carry six or seven soldiers. These are useful for escorting a convoy. There were Pinzgauers arriving, but Puch vehicles too, because other units had those. Different units had different vehicles, and these vehicles were used to secure the convoy. There may have been Campagnolas as well, because those too were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal with numbers. We know from your record that there 175 officers and men brought to Ovcara, and there is no secret, from Mitnica. Now, we've got 175 prisoners of war. Can you remember in general terms how many military police individuals were securing those 175 prisoners of war? Can you give us an idea of the figures involved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: No. The reason is when the vehicles arrived and pulled over, I was called by my commander, Vojnovic. I talked to him and to Captain Karanfilov. We were some way from the scene. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic told me those were prisoners from Mitnica; Captain Karanfilov was in charge of their transport. He said they would be spending the night right there and that I would be receiving any further orders from Captain Karanfilov. The number of people who arrived or the military policemen escorting them, these were not something that I was able to observe at the time or have a clear idea of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's deal, if we may, with your meeting with Captain Karanfilov. How do you know that his name was Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic called me to one side and introduced me to Captain Karanfilov. He told me was his formal position was, but I did not memorise that. I was told about what the entire procedure would be, that those people had surrendered at Mitnica, that they had been disarmed, that we needed to organise a security system under the Geneva Conventions, that there was to be no mistreatment of these people, that no force should be used against them, no violence, that those people should not be insulted and so on and so forth. I was also told there were a certain number of officers there, military officers, who should be treated in keeping with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. I was told that Karanfilov would, from now on, be in command of the entire operation for as long as security continued to be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to clarify, if I may, please, your answer at 79, 14, to assist the Court. Your answer is as follows: "Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic called me to one side and introduced me to Captain Karanfilov. He told me what his formal position was, but I did not memorise that." Now, who is the "he," is it Vojnovic or is it Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: I knew Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, and he was my superior. He introduced me to Captain Karanfilov and the other way around too. He introduced me to Captain Karanfilov. This was an introduction between two military officers. And then Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic told me that I would be taking any further orders and tasks from Captain Karanfilov. I hope this is sufficient explanation for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When Vojnovic told you that, was that in the presence of Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the convoy arrived we were called to one side. When I say "we," I mean Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, Captain Karanfilov and I. There may have been another officer there, but I can't remember. Essentially the conversation was between Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, Captain Karanfilov and myself. Captain Karanfilov was introduced to me, I was introduced to him. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic then said that I would be taking any further orders and assignments from Captain Karanfilov.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us that you were told by Vojnovic that Karanfilov would from now on be in command of the entire operation for as long as the security continued to be provided. Did Karanfilov agree to that particular statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The introductions over, Karanfilov said to me that he had 185 soldiers there who -- 175 soldiers there, most of them Croats, that there were six officers among them, and that one of the officers was carrying a small Stanley knife, that everybody else had been disarmed, but it had been agreed that this officer would keep this small pocket knife. And he said I shouldn't worry about this. He said I shouldn't check the prisoners for weapons again. All I was to do was put them up in the hangar and get on with the security regime. So that was the exchange between the three of us. And we were standing some distance from the actual scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long did this conversation occur, in general terms? How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I really can't remember. Couldn't have been under 10 minutes. Introductions were made, an order was given, another task were assigned, was given, so it can't possibly have been under 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you were speaking to Vojnovic and Karanfilov, was it daylight or night-time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: They arrived at about 1600 hours. There was still natural light, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you have a clear view of Karanfilov when you were speaking to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Of course. We were a metre or two apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And finally, before I go on to another topic, to which unit did Karanfilov belong?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't remember that point what unit he belonged to, even though I was told exactly which unit he was from. The only thing that I remember is that he was a security guy, as we say, in the army. So he belonged to the security organ. In our jargon, we would just say that he was a security man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to refer now to a document, but before I do so, I just want to lay the groundwork for the compilation of the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, I think it's right to say that you have what I will call a mid-size red military notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And do you have it with you in court?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us just deal with the military notebook itself. We can deal with the specifics in a moment. But in general terms, was that a notebook that you compiled throughout your period at Vukovar and indeed other locations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to deal, please, with page 48 of that notebook. And it is 65 ter Exhibit 125. And the number should be 7205 going right through to 7214, but the actual document or page that I wish to refer to should be numbered page 48, and that is the natural numbering on the book itself. Well, it's certainly showing on my screen, but it's almost illegible. Is it possible to be turned around so it can be read? Yes. Can we just look, please? I think it's right to say that it is page 48, top left-hand corner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have some sympathy, you having to get your glasses out to look at it. Would you have your original document there? Could you produce it, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is it in your handbag?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And to aid your reading, can you go to the top left-hand corner of the page? It's page 48.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you just read out, please, what that actually says?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: It says "OS" and then "Sremski front," "srem front" in quotations, "Sid," and then beneath that it says "Captain Karanfilov."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why did you write that down, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: When Captain Karanfilov was introduced to me and when I was introduced to him, I was told, or Captain Karanfilov told me that if I needed anything during the night, because he was not going to be at Ovcara the whole time, if I needed anything, I could find him at the elementary school Sremski front, in Sid, which I wrote down just as a reminder to me where I could find him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who gave you this name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: The elementary school Sremski front in Sid was something that Captain Karanfilov told me as the place where I would be able to find him if I needed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just when we're on the topic, if we look at the page we can see numbers on the right-hand page, it's page 49, top right-hand corner, we can see numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and -- now, can we just deal with that page, please? To what does that relate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: When the introductions were finished, and when we finished our conversation, Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, Captain Karanfilov and myself, we went to the first bus. Six persons were taken out from the first bus, and Captain Karanfilov, myself and these six people talked. And Captain Karanfilov introduced me to them, and introduced them to me, one by one. Again, in front of them he told me that I had to act in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, that these were senior officers who had been at Mitnica, and that one of them had a small pocket knife that they could keep, and one of them confirmed that. I don't know which one that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, please, with the actual names, the six names that you've written down? Who is the first one, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Then they introduced themselves to me and I noted their names down. First I wrote the last name, the name of the father, and then the first name, and then below that I wrote the date of -- or the year of birth. These six persons whose names I wrote down, next to their name it wasn't their rank but the tasks that they had. So with the name Karaula I put commander; with Komsic, I put commander of a company; Mandic, commander of a company; Nujic, commander of a company; Osust, commander of the escort platoon; and then on the next page where I wrote down the name of Brajcic, I did not write down his function. These were the first six people that I met and whose names I wrote down. Six officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we just deal with the generalities for a moment. Did Karanfilov indicate if he would return to Ovcara to deal with this group of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: When all the soldiers came out, now we're talking about a much later period, when they were put up at the hangar, Captain Karanfilov told me that he was going to go and deal with some other assignments, and then if he managed to, we would see each other in the course of the night; if not, then probably the next day at around 8.00 in the morning when some international organisations were expected to arrive, such as the Red Cross. And after that the further transport of these prisoners of war had to be organised to get them to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about Karanfilov, you told us about Vojnovic, obviously yourself. Were there any other officers present when these prisoners of war were brought to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: There were many officers there, but as I said, I wasn't really paying much attention to the number of officers, to their ranks. They were senior officers, lower ranking officers, but I didn't pay attention to that, because none of them interfered in this whole thing. The conversation proceeded only between Vojnovic, Karanfilov and myself, and then later these six officers, the Croatian prisoners joined the conversation. So throughout that time I was just talking and receiving orders from Captain Karanfilov.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Tell me, how long it take to offload the prisoners of war into the hangar, in very general terms, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: From half an hour to 45 minutes. When the first bus was empty, it moved along, and then the next bus came, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We are coming to the end of the day. I would like to just finish this small area or topic. When all the prisoners were placed inside the hangar, how many persons, how many soldiers were used to actually guard them or control them? Can you give us a figure?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: If we count just the military policemen, there were about 20 of them. There was also a certain number of officers there who were obliged to help in the security with other soldiers, not military policemen, but other soldiers. Altogether approximately we had about 60 conscripts who, at that time, were working on this security. Including the officers who were present and who were entrusted with assisting in the whole operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we are talking about controlling these prisoners of war through the evening, night, into the next morning, did that number of 60 remain generally constant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the number, more or less. The thing is that we would also go to Negoslavci and come back for the simple reason that we had to provide food and water for the group. Whatever we were able to get we brought back and distributed to them. We would go back and return, but more or less the group was compact. At any given time, one group of people was on guard duty and another group was resting. So at any given moment they were always 20 people on active duty. The others were resting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the ones who were resting, were they in a position to assist, if trouble occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The general idea was for them to be completely separate in a different room, but it turned out that because of the cold it was not so easy to provide another room that could more or less be warm enough. So then I decided that we should all be in that one room. All of those who were waiting were in that area where there was still some straw left. There was a number of soldiers who were in front of the building, and they were the ones that had to be replaced more often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, just a short intervention for the transcript. Page 86, line 24, the witness said that there were always between 15 or 20 people on active guard duty while in the transcript it says 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore, is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, the notebook, I would ask the court officer to take possession of that overnight, if you would. The court registry officer. Thank you. And if counsel wish to view it, they may make arrangements with the court officer, because it will remain in his possession, and it will be able to be carried on, used again tomorrow morning by the witness. Now, we resume tomorrow morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of May, 2006, at 9.30 a.m.
